rewrites.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical. For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is among the most protective documented: since Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; the documented Synthia Kavanagh litigation — a transgender prisoner's court proceedings over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — shows placement and care are litigable in Canadian courts. The caveats are documented practice gaps: a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault; a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; and no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the federal identity-based placement rule. For the rare visitor who ends up in custody, the documented standard is identity-based placement with functioning judicial recourse — the abuse allegations are the practice gap to weigh.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent climate: the 2017 protections were framed as national leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash, and the resident-facing provincial school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks (Alberta, Saskatchewan) are the visible policy turbulence in an otherwise settled national framework.

Custody-axis policy context: the prime minister's promised review of transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity is federal administrative machinery rather than a visitor-facing protection.

Litigation history on the custody axis: Wikipedia's article on lawyer Barbara findlay records that she represented transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation concerning gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — evidence that Canadian trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care were litigated in court, though the source gives no dates or final outcome, so the case is thin on specifics. Outside the prison axis, no litigation flux is reported in the current sources: the 2012 human-rights shadow submission predates the 2017 protections (gender identity/expression added to the human-rights act and criminal code; conversion-therapy prohibitions from 2021/22) and is superseded.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Provincial self-declaration legal gender recognition, the federal X marker, and the Alberta/Saskatchewan school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks are resident-facing; the 2022 survey data describes residents.

The current sources add resident-facing legal infrastructure: a 2016 provincial reform created a document-update pathway (self-declaration plus a doctor's letter, the surgery requirement removed); provincial human-rights commission policy guidance supports sexual-orientation discrimination complaints; the 2012 shadow submission documented the era's trans-protection gaps.

The custody findings are resident-facing: the federal identity-based placement rule, the 12-month sex-reassignment-surgery consideration, and the documented conditions (the 2022 Nova Scotia correctional-officer study finding officers generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with concerns about risk to other prisoners; the 2022 CTV report alleging a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners and higher sexual-assault victimisation) govern or describe residents held in custody — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention, and the Kavanagh litigation is a prisoner's case.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals; the current sources do not address marriage or partner-travel questions for a visitor in any detail.

Unverifiable in the current sources: the 2024 national hate-crime analysis page and the 2022 federal survey page were not retrievable at research time (redirect loop; timeout), so the figures above rest on the record's summary text and the retrievable source claims.

Prison axis: no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the federal identity-based placement rule; the CTV abuse allegations are reported allegations rather than adjudicated findings; and the Kavanagh case's dates and final outcome are not given in the source, so its precedential weight is unverifiable.
rewrites.notes: rw003 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (Wikipedia LGBTQ people in prison — Canada section: federal identity-based placement post-C-16, 12-month surgery consideration, CTV abuse allegations, Nova Scotia officer study, no special-unit/solitary detail; Barbara findlay Wikipedia — Synthia Kavanagh placement/care litigation, thin on dates/outcome) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024). The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction, and there is no rollback movement.

The consequence axis of an arrest is only partly documented. Detention law is cantonal: the one explicit placement rule on record is Basel-Stadt's detention law (Justizvollzugsgesetz, adopted 13 November 2019), whose separation provisions require female and male detainees to be separated and stipulate that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate allowed to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No national placement rule, trans-prisoner case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record, so placement for a detained trans visitor is a cantonal question that is otherwise undocumented — and detention under a standard with no national guarantee and an explicit deviation power cannot be assumed to follow identity-based placement in every canton.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Placement-framework context: detention law is cantonal, and Basel-Stadt's November 2019 inclusion of gender identity in its detention law — the only such rule documented in this record — was a canton-level measure aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities; the national Wikipedia overview records the vote but documents no federal placement rule, so the institutional signal is cantonal rather than a visitor-facing national protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-declaration LGR process (binary only, no non-binary marker) and the employer duty of care are resident-facing administrative/employment law.

The documented detention rule is resident-facing: Basel-Stadt's JVG governs detainees held in that canton, requiring separation of female and male detainees with the caveat that the detained person's gender identity is respected as far as possible and that the prison directorate may deviate in consultation with the referring authority — a standard resident prisoners stand under; a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention, and outside Basel-Stadt no placement standard is documented.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Switzerland's principal travel risks (mountain/alpine hazards, road safety) affect all travellers.

Prison axis: the JVG applies only to Basel-Stadt; no national (federal) trans-prisoner placement rule, Swiss trans-prisoner case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented, so placement practice in the other cantons and the practical operation of the 'as far as possible' standard and its deviation power are unverifiable here — a gap that cannot be read as a protected standard.
rewrites.notes: rw003 VIS: folded verified prison-axis sources (Basel-Stadt JVG 2019: gender identity respected 'as far as possible' in placement with directorate deviation power; Wikipedia Switzerland overview: no national placement rule, no case law, no special units, no solitary/segregation practice) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the only prison-axis source in this record — Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page — contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners, nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons. In a state with no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection and an inadequate police response to organised targeting, an undocumented placement practice cannot be read as a protected one: a detained trans visitor would be held in a prison system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Reputation and regional context: long considered the region's tolerant outlier, the country's standing is now in sharp downshift. A regional rights framework exists — a continental resolution marking a decade of advancing LGBT+ rights — though its protective operation here is not evidenced in this record.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing data: a 2015 academic study of trans-feminine people (travestis) found they face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and they have been underserved by the country's rights groups, which distanced themselves. The 2023 official report recorded three community deaths in the year and a transgender man beaten while walking in a suburb of the largest city; it also notes authorities handled complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

The prison-axis documentation gap is itself resident-facing: no Ivorian rule, case or report on where trans detainees are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record — Human Rights Watch's country page contains no such finding — so detained trans residents stand under an undocumented practice that no source describes as protective.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The main late-2024 reporting on the hunt wave was not retrievable at research time — the news article returns a hard error — so the wave's details rest on the source summary and corroborating official reporting. A freshness flag notes that criminalisation language cited in 2023-era reports no longer appears in the current overview; whether such provisions persist is unresolved and needs rechecking.

Prison axis: the only prison-axis source is thin — Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page has no usable finding on where trans detainees are housed ('LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link, and no HRW publication is listed on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons) — and with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, that absence cannot be read as a signal of any protected placement standard.
rewrites.notes: rw003 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (HRW country page: thin, no usable trans-prisoner housing finding) into visible fields as thin-data consequence evidence per LANE_SPECS rule 8b; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as a policy-practice gap: since June 2017 the Justice Ministry has announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility — relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, with a census of self-identified trans prisoners ordered and an exclusive module for trans people under consideration. The practice side diverged: a June 2019 investigation found a trans woman serving a ~6-year sentence at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, where the prison offered only two options — 'you're a man or a woman here' — and she recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) that a custodian witnessed; the Justice Ministry then counted 23 transgender people in the national system. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a formal identity-based choice policy whose documented practice still placed trans women in men's facilities in 2019, with violence and custodial inaction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Marriage equality since 2020 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

The 2017 placement policy was presented as modelled on Spain's system, with protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016 — institutional context for the choice policy rather than a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The administrative name/photo ID process (which does not change the sex marker) and universal healthcare covering transition-related care are resident-facing.

The custody policy and its documented practice are resident-facing: the 2017 Justice Ministry choice policy (voluntary placement by gender identity, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, census ordered, exclusive module considered) and the 2019 counter-example — Stephanie, a trans woman serving ~6 years at a men's facility, told the prison offered only 'man or woman', recounting identity-targeted abuse including a rape at another facility witnessed by a custodian — govern prisoners; a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.

Prison axis: no Costa Rican data on trans special units or solitary/segregation practice is documented — the exclusive module was 'under consideration' in 2017 and whether it was ever built is unverifiable from these sources; how the 2017 choice policy operates today is likewise unverified, with the 2019 men's-facility placement the only documented practice point.
rewrites.notes: rw003 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (AmeliaRueda 2017: Justice Ministry identity-based voluntary placement choice, census order, exclusive module considered; CRHoy 2019: men's-facility placement counter-example, 23 trans prisoners counted) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis. For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the record's darkest documented element. Trans women in the country's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces: the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (an organisation working with them says there are many more), placement operates by birth sex/legal sex, and the protective 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations is used unevenly — one trans detainee was initially sent to a male pavilion with three other trans women rather than to it, and received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The sources document gender-identity discrimination, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers in custody, including the death of a trans woman during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space, a 2022 complaint over cruel and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio, 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings targeting breast/body implants, a 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman that drew calls for an independent investigation, and reporting that rapes and torture in custody are directed at prisoners' gender identity. The leading trans-rights organisation does not push a one-size placement rule — it advocates individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, citing a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty — so a detained trans visitor would face male-space placement under an unevenly applied protective standard with documented violence.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The framework's bedrock is the adjacent layer: the 2008 constitution's non-discrimination foundation (including sexual orientation and identity), the 2019 marriage-equality ruling, and a 2018 court order requiring the civil registry to register the child of a same-sex couple. Dated official context: a 2011 human-rights report documented discrimination based on sexual orientation among broader societal problems, and the platform notes that same-sex couples remain barred from adoption by a constitutional ban.

Custody-framework context: the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty predates the documented placement practice, and the leading trans-rights organisation's prison program deliberately advocates individualised housing decisions under Inter-American standards rather than a single placement rule — institutional context for the documented male-space practice, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2024 Civil Registry reform and the adolescent document-change rulings are resident-facing; the 27-murder toll and its inadequate state response fall on residents.

The adolescent rulings arose from a specific teenager's case that opened the path for other adolescents seeking legal recognition, and the 2024 reform's operative procedure came via the 2024 regulation of the identity law.

The documented custody conditions are resident-facing: trans women held in male pavilions, the protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly, and the documented deaths and abuse (the November 2021 massacre death at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male space, the 2022 complaint over treatment in Lago Agrio, the 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings, the 2026 death in State custody at El Encuentro maximum-security prison) all fall on residents held in the system — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance. The murder toll is a single organisation's documentation and the response assessment is that organisation's; the 2024-25 adolescent rulings are as reported and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Prison axis: the census count (73 trans women) and the 'prioritaria' practice are as reported by the cited investigations — how allocation to the protective pavilion is decided and how many trans women reach it is not documented, the implementation status of the 2016 protocol commitment is unverified, and no rule or case law fixing trans-prisoner placement (birth-sex vs identity) is on record beyond the documented practice itself.
rewrites.notes: rw003 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (Silueta X PrisioTrans 2011-2026 documentation: male-space placement, deaths, abuse allegations, individualised-placement advocacy; Pulitzer Center 2024 investigation: 73-count census, 'prioritaria' uneven use, male-pavilion placement) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.
